title: CBSA demoting border officers who permanently lost ability to use sidearm | CBC News
html:
Politics·New

CBSA demoting border officers who permanently lost ability to use sidearm

Union says officers still have value, agency points to responsible use of public funds

The Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) has informed 63 employees that they will have to take on new, lower-paid positions because of medical conditions that prevent them from carrying a sidearm.

The agency told CBC News in a statement that it is willing to offer temporary accommodations to employees who are unable to carry a firearm because of medical or psychological conditions.

However, when employees require permanent accommodation, it said they must be transferred "to a position for which carrying a firearm is not a condition of employment."

Several employees and their union are denouncing the planned demotions, saying that the affected border officers carry out duties that do not require the use of a firearm on a daily basis.

They also say the agency is penalizing experienced employees because of medical or psychological conditions, such as workplace injuries or mental and physical health issues that prevent them from requalifying for firearm use every two years.

The 63 officers affected by the measure represent 0.7 per cent of the 8,500 CBSA positions that require the ability to wear a sidearm.

Union calls process discriminatory, unfair

In a recent message to the employees, the CBSA warned that they would have to go through a "downward deployment without salary protection" as part of the "reasonable accommodation process."

"We think it's discriminatory, it's arbitrary and it's unfair," said Mark Weber, president of the Customs and Immigration Union.

One of the affected officers criticized the message as bureaucratic and impersonal.

Mark Weber is the president of the Customs and Immigration Union. He says the CBSA's decision is discriminatory. (Simon Lasalle/Radio-Canada)

"I felt like a file being closed, not a human being," the employee said.

The officer said they cried when they received the message telling them they would be getting a pay cut after years of service.

"The firearm never helped me do that job. My experience did. That experience didn’t disappear when I stopped being able to carry my gun," they said.

"I want to keep doing work that is important. I’m asking to be able to do that without being punished financially for having a medical disability."

The employee spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss their personal situation without their employer's permission.

In addition to the 63 officers being demoted, 14 employees on sick leave remain under review.

Another 36 officers have retired since January rather than lose the accommodations that allowed them to work in their current roles.

In all, 190 employees had been receiving workplace accommodations related to firearms. Aside from those facing demotion or who have already left, 27 were transferred to positions at the same level and 50 returned to their regular duties after receiving medical clearance.

The CBSA has 18,000 employees, including roughly 8,500 in front-line positions that require carrying a firearm, notably at border crossings and other ports of entry.

Dangerous work at CBSA includes intercepting illegal drugs, firearms and other prohibited goods at the border, as well as deporting individuals who are not authorized to be in Canada.

The use of force remains rare, with CBSA officers across the country drawing their sidearms an average total of 28 times a year.

Several employees who have been granted accommodations related to the carrying of firearms perform office work. (Radio-Canada)

In certain workplaces such as airports and postal centres, border services officers do not always carry their sidearm. Officers can also perform duties without carrying a gun, including working on the Nexus program, analyzing flight manifests and training new officers, according to the union.

A CBSA spokesperson said that "carrying protective and defensive equipment is intrinsically linked to the performance of duties" of border officers, including enforcing the law "when necessary."

"When an individual can no longer be fully armed or meet the requirements of their duties, the CBSA has a duty to accommodate them," said spokesperson Kelly Cameron.

However, she added the agency must spend public funds judiciously and ensure its employees meet the "essential requirements" of positions, including those that require being staffed by an armed officer.

"The CBSA is not required to permanently exempt an employee from performing the essential duties of their position or to create work that is not necessary," she said.

In its letter to the 63 employees who are still unable to carry a firearm, the CBSA stated that there are "no longer any suitable placement opportunities" at their current level.

At least one letter said that available placements would be shared "in the coming weeks."

Weber said the agency is needlessly depriving itself of long-serving employees with decades of experience.

"Essentially, they are being told by their employer that they no longer have value simply because they can no longer carry a firearm," he said.
summary: The Canada Border Services Agency has informed 63 employees that they will have to take on new, lower-paid positions because of medical conditions that prevent them from carrying a sidearm.
